title: "Chipewyan"
subtitle: "Canada"
region: "North America"
tags: [ethnography, north-america]

## Overview

The Chipewyan, also called the *Dënesųłı̨né*, are a Dene group of Indigenous Canadian people belonging to the Athabaskan language family. Their ancestors are identified with the Taltheilei Shale archaeological tradition, and they are part of the Northern Athabascan group of peoples. They live across the western Canadian Shield and the Northwest Territories, including northern parts of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan. Their territory includes the region around Great Slave Lake, Lake Athabasca, the Churchill River, the Athabasca River, Reindeer Lake and many other lakes and rivers. In August 2016, the listed First Nations band governments had a total registered membership of 25,519. The group’s folk-culture significance in the sources is especially connected with mobility, caribou hunting, fishing, fur trading, tepee living, clothing and the Denesuline language.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Parkas** — The name Chipewyan is explained through a Cree expression meaning “pointed hides” or “pointed skin,” referring to the cut and style of Chipewyan parkas.

**One-piece pants and moccasin outfits** — These formed part of the clothing worn when Chipewyan people were largely nomadic.

**Caribou clothing materials** — Caribou was historically a major source of materials for clothing.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

Historically, the Chipewyan wore one-piece pants and moccasin outfits. Their parkas are associated with the explanation of the name Chipewyan: the Cree expression refers to “pointed hides” or “pointed skin,” and to the cut and style of the parkas. Caribou was a major historical source of materials for clothing. The sources also state that Chipewyan people temporarily lived in tepees and that their clothing belonged to a largely nomadic way of life.

### Architecture

The Chipewyan were historically organized into small bands and temporarily lived in tepees. Their groups moved between winter and summer camps in the boreal forest and around the many lakes of their territory.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

In the subarctic trade, Chipewyan people exchanged furs and hides for metal tools, guns and cloth. The sources also mention modern nets, tools and transportation in connection with fishing and caribou hunting, but provide no catalogue of forms, manufacturing techniques or decorative practices.

## Music & performance

The language sources describe Denesuline as a Northern Athabaskan language and record its consonants, vowels, diphthongs and two tones. No information is supplied about music at hunting camps, gatherings, weddings, funerals, ceremonies or other occasions.

## Festivals & rituals

They do describe seasonal movement between winter and summer camps and subsistence activities including hunting, trapping, fishing and gathering. Caribou hunting was historically important, and the Sayisi Dene were notable for hunting migratory caribou. In the 1970s, the “Duck Lake Dene” chose self-reliance and returned to caribou hunting after relocation. The government forcibly relocated them in 1956 to Churchill and a small village north of Churchill called North Knife River; their relocation is commemorated by the Dene Memorial in Churchill, Manitoba.

## Foodways

Caribou was historically a major source of food as well as clothing and tool materials. Chipewyan subsistence also included fishing, trapping and gathering in the boreal forest and around the many lakes of their territory. Modern Chipewyan people continue traditional subsistence practices including fishing and caribou hunting, although the sources state that these practices have been modernized through the use of modern nets, tools and transportation.

## Oral tradition & literature

They do record the historical figure Thanadelthur, described as a young woman who early in the 18th century helped her people establish peace with the Cree and become involved in the fur trade. The sources also list Matonabbee, Matooskie, Thánadëltth'ér, Louis Riel, Jimmy Herman and Alex Janvier among notable Chipewyans or people with Chipewyan connections. The language sources mention a Chipewyan translation of the New Testament, *Didi gothi testementi*, published in London in 1881. No contemporary literary revival or preservation project is described beyond the listed language resources.

## Language & religion

Denesuline, also called Chipewyan or *Dënesųłinë́*, belongs to the Northern Athabaskan branch of the Athabaskan language family. The ethnonym *Dënesųłinë́ yatié* or *Dëne Sųłıné Yatıé* is also given, while *Dëne* is a shorter form. In the 2011 Canada Census, 11,860 people chose Dënesųłinë́ as their mother tongue. The language has official status only in the Northwest Territories, alongside eight other aboriginal languages. Speakers use different dialects but understand each other; the sources describe a “k” dialect and a “t” dialect, with examples from Fond du Lac, *Gąnı kuę́*. Dënesųłinë́ has 39 consonants, six differing vowel qualities, 24 phonemic vowels and two tones, high and low.

## Sources & further reading

- “Chipewyan language,” *Wikipedia*: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chipewyan_language
